title: Pasta with Tomato-Based Sauce, Cheese and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with tomato-based sauce, cheese and meat is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of boiled pasta, coated with a tomato sauce, sprinkled with grated cheese and mixed with pieces of cooked or fried meat. The meal combines carbohydrates, protein and fat, providing a balanced source of energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce is often made from ripe tomatoes, olive oil, onion and herbs, making it a rich source of lycopene.
The tradition of pairing pasta with meat dates back to 19th‑century Italy, when meat ragù became popular.
Cheese added to the dish is usually Parmesan or mozzarella, giving it aroma and boosting calcium content.
Pasta cooks quickly: most shapes reach al dente in 8‑12 minutes after the water boils.
In restaurants the dish is commonly served as “spaghetti Bolognese,” though home cooks use any pasta shape.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: The combination of carbs from pasta and protein from meat provides sustained satiety and supports energy levels.

items.title: Rich in lysine
items.content: Meat supplies lysine, an essential amino acid important for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Grated cheese adds calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Enriched pasta and meat provide B1, B3 and B6 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because the dish combines carbs, fats and proteins, it can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese often contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Meat and cheese may contain saturated fats, which in excess can raise cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, optionally topping with extra cheese and fresh herbs. A drizzle of olive oil or a pinch of spices can be added to taste. It pairs well with bread or a side salad for a balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pasta in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months after cooling.
